title: From Human to AI: Cognitive Mechanisms Underlying the Associations between Insecure Interpersonal Attachment Styles and Human-AI Emotional Engagement
description: Attachment styles have long been shown to shape how individuals form and maintain interpersonal relationships. Extending this perspective to human-AI interaction, the present study examined whether and how individuals’ interpersonal attachment styles were linked to their human-AI emotion-related behaviors and attachment. We further tested whether this process was mediated by cognitive perceptions related to AI’s emotional capacity (i.e., perceived uniqueness of AI) and moderated by individuals’ cognitive disposition to view non-living entities as human-like (i.e., dispositional anthropomorphism). Participants were a regionally representative sample of 1,406 undergraduate students (Mage = 18.98 years, SD = 1.25; 40% male) recruited from 26 universities in Shanghai, China, using a stratified random sampling procedure. Participants reported on their interpersonal attachment styles, perceived uniqueness of AI, anthropomorphism, and two indicators of emotional engagement with AI: personal disclosure and emotional attachment. Results showed that both interpersonal attachment anxiety and attachment avoidance were positively associated with perceived uniqueness of AI, which was in turn associated with greater personal disclosure and stronger emotional attachment to AI. Anthropomorphism further moderated the association between perceived uniqueness of AI and emotional engagement, such that these associations were stronger among individuals with higher levels of anthropomorphism. Similarly, moderated mediation analyses indicated that the indirect effects of interpersonal attachment orientations on emotional engagement with AI through perceived uniqueness of AI were amplified at higher levels of anthropomorphism. Overall, the findings suggest that human-AI emotional engagement may be shaped by both individuals’ human-human attachment-related orientations and their psychological construal of AI as a human-like, relationally meaningful interaction partner.

title: Attitudes and Affect towards Statistics in First Year Psychology Studends - a Bayesian Approach
description:
Statistics is regarded as one of the most difficult and frightening subjects by psychology
students. The present study develops a Bayesian framework for a more comprehensive
understanding of students´ attitudes and affect towards statistics, their development and
predictors. Furthermore, an extensive collection of related constructs was raised and analysed
psychometrically. In a longitudinal design, data of first year psychology students was collected
via online surveys at the beginning of the lectures, midst-semester and after course completion.
Four Bayesian models were fitted to inspect response patterns, pairwise item correlations and
construct change over time. In a final multilevel generalized linear varying effects model, the
effects of Statistics Anxiety on Affective Behaviours towards statistics were analysed.
Psychometric analysis yielded surprising results, as most instruments revealed insufficient
properties in the present sample. Comparative analyses revealed that Affective Behaviours
increased over the course of the semester, and Statistics Anxiety decreased. The relationship
between Affective Behaviours and Statistics Anxiety was complex, as some subscales were
correlated positively against expectations. In conclusion, the present study developed a
Bayesian framework for comprehensive data analysis, presents preliminary results of Affective
Behaviours and Statistics Anxiety and discusses a potential reliability risk in the field due to
deficient reporting of psychometric analyses.

title: Robust circular cluster-based statistics for respiration-brain coupling
description: The rapidly developing research field of brain-body neuroscience faces methodological challenges, as analysts continue to develop new analysis strategies for robust statistics in the absence of established best practices. This quest for robust statistics is further complicated by the (naturally) circular data involved in the study of phase-locked effects, e.g. in respiration-brain coupling. Circularity of respiratory data particularly affects the problem of multiple comparisons in phase-related inferential statistics. In this tutorial, we propose a robust pipeline for respiration-related analyses based on a circular extension of cluster-based permutation testing we developed. We highlight and offer guidance on critical parameters in the analysis, systematically compare various approaches being used in the field today, and provide open-access software code for flexible use and future development of our proposed pipeline.
